"Inferring the rules" is itself 3 distinct problems: exploring game space to collect data, turning the data into causal models of game mechanics, and inferring the goal(s). So in total you have 4 problems to solve:

- Exploration
- Modeling
- Goal setting
- Planning + execution (in the general case these are 2 different problems, but in ARC 3 they are basically merged into one)

The difficulty breakdown of each subproblem depends on the environment. But on average it should look something like:

- Exploration: 20% difficulty
- Modeling: 65% difficulty
- Goal setting: 10% difficulty (very game dependent, can be quite hard for some games and trivial for others)
- Planning + execution: 5% difficulty (mostly kicks in on latter levels; initial levels have ~0% difficulty on this axis)

I have been thinking along this lines too and wanted to add some observations.

I think at least six distinct stages are necessary for 'intelligent' solving of a game level.

1. Perceiver: reduction of pixel world into grid world (or list of entities and their spatial locations)
2. Scientist: learning of the properties and functions of each entity or each interaction of avatar with that entity.
3. Game Modeler: learning GOAL of the game, what gives final reward or intermediate reward, what punishes temporarily or terminally; figuring out PURPOSE of each entity or interaction in this path.
4. Milestone and Subroutine learner: ability to re-see the finished episodes not as a single chain of actions, but as sequence of state-changing milestones and the actions needed to go from each to the other.
5. Planner: Specifying in a new unsolved level through 'mental' simulation with current understanding, a solution in the form of sorties or subgoals or milestones.
6. Execution: Decomposing the sorties in an actual situation to arrive at action sequence - and using perception/scientist/modeling work again if there are new unknowns that thwart the plan.

To make this concrete, in the locksmith game. (SPOILER for those who have not played it)
1. Perceiver does not 'see' 64x64 image frame. They see playable area, HUD of battery life and lives, they see key map and lock and room.
2. Scientist (Exploration and Experimentation) finds out that touching a modifier changes the key shape or size or color. and that without that match touching lock is useless.
3. Game Modeler figures out that goal of the game is to transform key to match the target on door and approach the door (on level 1)
4. Milestone Subroutine learner learns where to go and what to do to change color, change shape or change orientation.
5. Planner first recognizes the sequence of milestones to solve the level. 
6. Execution simulates mentally what is needed for each milestone and milestone by milestone reaches the goal, recovering form mistakes.

The reason why humans excel in the games is we do not search in action space. We do not even search in state space. The planner searches in the sortie space or milestone space.
They done say move left move right in their solution. They say go to forge change shape, go to palette, paint, then rotate and go to door.
Planning happens at very sparse synthesis.

Each of the first 3 stages in a module in a data reduction cascade - it dramatically re-presents what data is worth paying attention to and transforms from spatial coordinates to invariant graph coordinates.

Perceiver transforms from pixel-space to grid space (condensing a 5x5 avatar or entity into a single point symbol)
Scientist connects which state-actions are of use and creates a state-action space with transition causal chains.
Game modeler and Milestone learner consolidate this information into a goal-back-driven tree that can help planner/executor derive programs.

Until the perceiver and scientist subset and re-present the pixel world into a state space, efficient game learning/planning/execution is impossible.

The reason chess and go play work so well is because they are already abstract grid worlds and further humans incorporate game model and milestone learning into search engines and planning becomes action-space search, which is actually a shame or cheating form of intelligence. brute force once decision tree is setup with heuristics to reduce burden a bit.

ARC-AGI-3 clearly exposes this gap and adding the action-budget is the brilliant stroke, because it forces us to realize that key to human efficiency is the ability to create transform spaces of perception and cognition WELL BEFORE game modeling begins. A possible 1000x data reduction from pixel worlds to object lists to rule-chains that are game-agnostic so that game goal discovery and semantic role labeling of entities can happen on this already small space. Game grammar induction.

Across game levels, we can then see which of the knowledge and skill and subroutines gained in a previous level carries over and what is new to be learned.

--

Modeling (in @fchollet note) I would split into world-modeling and game-modeling and bundle the goal discovery into that.
Planning and execution - I will split into two, one that outlines milestone reaching and remains stable guide for the execution-planner and executor.

--

To summarize, a good solution architecture REQUIRES where in symbolic fashion or neurosymbols:

- Perceiver: pixel grids to symbolic grid or entity lists
- Scientist: entity lists to rule lists
- Game Model: Goal, Milestone, Subroutines
- Planner: scene to milestone sequence and subgoal states
- Execution: Pathfinding from milestone to milestone with recovery from mistakes

This view also restates Comprehension as goal-directed compression of information. Compression itself is not as important as relevance filtering. Intelligence is the recognition of events that cause world-state to change for better or worse and noticing and remembering and consolidating the action/context/happening chains that lead each such state change. Intelligence is ability to chain them at will to reach a goal.

( I am planning to post this also as a separate discussion, which I plan to update frequently with my experiments and results)

replies.rawMarkdown:
Yes, but the relief I am seeing in my own instropective play is that each stage builds on previous stage and feeds back to it and refines it, but they are quite self contained otherwise.
In other words, once perceiver is fairly stable and customized for scientist, perceiver is frozen until next level new elements get introduced. Likewise once game comprehender understands the game goals and rules, scientist is pretty much done. Each stage that becomes an encoder-decoder that creates compact representation of what is necessary and complete to the next.

One big new think I am finding is that Planning happens in a graph (of entity relationships) that does not have spatial grid in mind. Execution happens in a grid world! In other words Planner says, rotate the key, change its color and shape and proceed to lock, executor translates it to real world and incorporates obstacle avoidance, etc. This is postponement of details that not only reduces cognitive load, it serves to create approximate solutions that can represent a manifold not a list of paths. This 'vagueness' of language is the virtue, aka abstraction.

Another point I might add, is that I still don't think a solution to ARC-3 would be yet AGI for this reason:

My belief is all the games will be able to be solved with combining known domain specific algorithms (maze search, jigsaw, symmetry matching...)

But, one could imagine a game that is equivalent to solving some hard unsolved math problem. (e.g. twin primes conjecture). And that cannot be solved just by algorithmically combining known piror algorithms but requires a "leap of thinking". Specifically, hard symbolic manipulation, analogy, generalisation and more. The key is the complexity of the world-model they can build. (And how self-refrenetial it is).

But we don't even have to go that far. I think even a moderately hard Sokoban puzzle might defeat the best AI's here. 

I could be wrong and that the AI's that solve ARC-3 are indeed so general that they could be applied to reasearch-type questions but I have my doubts at this stage. Thoughts?

I am not entirely sure that the exact goal is to claim AGI. It seems to me more about: what kinds of problems do we have to solve to get there, and what might some of those solutions be?

While combinations of known solutions might get AI through individual levels, getting AI through the games with -a good score- is likely to require closer to what a human does. A human doesn't pattern match against every game they've ever played and decide on an algorithm. Well, this human doesn't. :) 

The test games look just enough like other games that treating the test games as if they -are- those games is its own specific form of trap, which the replays of the reasoning models that include their reasoning demonstrate. 

Personally, having played somanygames in my life, I see games as a form of language, so this is like "how quickly can you learn and apply this language?"

Actions are literally verbs. "Things on the board" are nouns. What happens when you apply verbs to the nouns teaches the grammar (game mechanics). 

Not all of the nouns are important, so which ones even matter, and is that situational? What is it about those pieces that makes you identify them as "mattering," and how can you impart that to a system that you can't coach after the run has started? 

Well-designed games, which these so far seem to be, don't expect you to know everything starting out. They give you a starting point and a list of actions and are like "GLHF" (good luck, have fun). 

When you first take an action, a person immediately knows more, even if they don't understand it. That leads to subconscious (sometimes conscious if the game's -really- hard) hypotheses that get tested, verified or negated, reformed. In the process, the mechanics reveal themselves over time. 

Not only that, but as you're absorbing the game's language, you can (frequently) apply it to later rounds. But doing so can either be easy (I see the same piece again, that's probably the thing I'm moving because last round involved moving a piece to another piece, and I see things that relate to the same goal state) or hard (okay, this level looks nothing like the first, what is it that I learned the last level that I could apply here). 

What I've been trying to do is to realize what I notice as I'm playing a level that I may be taking for granted. I identify things that look important. I do a thing to find out what happens. I update what's important based on that and the current board state, which may be radically different. 

I keep going until either I win, or I look at the game and go "nah" because I -know- what I'm supposed to do, and I don't want to because it's too fiddly. :D 

That's... not exactly how things work for AI. AI doesn't have memory, it needs that. It doesn't inherently have "I pressed left 3 times and some bar decreased in 3 times" because, unless you're just throwing everything at it, it doesn't inherently -know- it has done the same thing before (ever). 

To me, one of the issues is reliably getting clean enough information to determine what's important. Deterministic methods don't hold up well to the games' variety, and vision models I've tried haven't been precise enough. I'm currently trying to find a balance that can provide comprehension about what a distinct piece might be while also being precise enough that it can be used consistently in reasoning (within a level). 

What works for me--naming each piece 'this thingie' or 'that thingie'--isn't going to work for AI because it's not specific enough. I'm really associating the terms (even when I reuse them) with specific combinations of pixels that I've identified as meaningfully related, even though I haven't described them meaningfully (to anyone else). 

After that, it's about surfacing the relevant information at the right time--how to make the models pay attention to what's really important and/or impart some sense of what that is? 

And then, it's about generalizing. "I hit left, bar got smaller, I hit left, bar got smaller, I hit up, bar got smaller" is mechanical, state-based observation, not "when I hit one of the directional keys, the bar will get smaller." 

I mean, you can only have those kinds of observations in the first place if you know both "left is last thing that happened" and also "the bar is smaller now than it was last turn" at the same time. 

Holding the whole history of a level (much less a whole game) is going to be a lot to process. We don't work like that. Personally, I note the bar decreasing and go "okay, I'll pay attention to that if it seems to get low and I don't think I'm near the goal." 

But that kind of generalizing is one of the challenges. 

To top it all off, to get a -good- score, it isn't simply enough to win the level. If you aren't able to apply -something- to the next one, you'll be stuck wasting moves rediscovering things you should "already know." So we also have to solve how to store and surface that information. 

I could be wrong about all this, by the way. :) It's just my understanding, and why I find the problem space so fascinating. 

I also want to compliment the games' designer(s). They're benevolently evil in a specific sort of way, and I'm here for it.

comments.rawMarkdown:
BTW. Interpreting the puzzle from the rules seems to be something an LLM is really good at. (Sometimes!) 
For example I asked chatGPT:
```python
Intrpret this puzzle: 
A 100x100 white grid with 2 red squares and 2 green squares. 
Legal move: when a red square is next to any other, turn that square red and the original red square white. 
Win: No green squares left.
```
Answer from ChatGPT:
```python
[...]
🧠 Key insight

Red squares behave like mobile agents that can:

Move around the board
“Overwrite” other colors (including green)

So effectively:

A red square can walk onto a green square and erase it
❗ Important constraint

You only ever have 2 red squares at a time (since moving one removes it from its original spot).

🎯 What’s the goal?

Remove all green squares (i.e., turn them red at some point).

💡 Can you always win?

Yes — and here’s why:

Each red square can move freely across the grid (like a sliding piece).
There are only 2 green squares.
You have 2 independent red movers.

So:

Send each red square toward a green square.
When a red steps onto a green, that green is eliminated.
Repeat until both greens are gone.
...

```

Which is exactly right! Trying to write code that could recognise this from the rules is much harder (but perhaps still worth doing). 
So at least in this simple case, LLMs seem to be a good recognition tool.

edit: Although it did miss something out: If the two green "goals" are close to one of the red "movers". Then that mover should collect both goals, that would be most optimum.

firstMessage.rawMarkdown:
In the past couple of months I have been creating a "general puzzle solver", where you enter the legal moves and win-conditions and it tries to solve it. Mainly with BFS, Mote-Carlo, state-hashing, and constraint-propagation methods. So this worked quite well for mazes, fox-chicken-corn-farmer puzzle, zebra-puzzle, tower-of-hanoi, sudoku, slitherlink, other pencil puzzles, 8-sliding puzzle,  8-queens, knights move, Tic-tac-toe, 4-coloring map, and a few more.

So the first thing I realised was that many simple "classic" AI problems don't need much reasoning and can be solved with tree-search, constraint propogation, and state-hashing and backtracking. Basically brute force. And this is not to be overlooked as it forms the backbone of any algorithm.

The second thing I realised was that it is easy to find counter examples for which this breaks. The simplest example is this:

A 100x100 white grid with 2 red squares and 2 green squares.

Legal move: when a red square is next to any other, turn that square red and the original red square white.

Win: No green squares left.

Just using tree-search and state-hashing is infeasible. The key to this is, I believe, is recognition of the problem. We have to recognise that this can be interpreted as 2 red agents and 2 goals. Then pick an algorithm (A* search with distance heuristic) to solve.

Other more general techniques are:

(1) Invariant finding: Noticing all moves fix the number of red squraes at 2 and green squares can only deplete. [This can be a bit tricky since some things are invariant for a certain time only]

(2) Splitting the problem: We notice we can pair up each red square with each green square and solve this as two concurrent puzzles. Also hard to recognise.

Some other observations:

People have studied this area in 

(1) General Game Playing (GGP)

(2) Planning Problems (PDDL/STRIPS)

One general thing from PDDL is the idea of ignoring delete lists to get a good admissible heuristic.

One of the hardest games to solve that is just at the edge of human solvability is Sokoban.

The general idea is just like there is not one general algorithm to solve any math problem, there will not be any one algorithm to solve any puzzle. So the idea is to use recognition and mix-and-match domain specific algorithms.

ARC-3 is a bit different in that you have to infer the rules. But once inferred you still have to have a good algorithm to solve it. So it's two hard problems in one!

firstMessage.content:
In the past couple of months I have been creating a "general puzzle solver", where you enter the legal moves and win-conditions and it tries to solve it. Mainly with BFS, Mote-Carlo, state-hashing, and constraint-propagation methods. So this worked quite well for mazes, fox-chicken-corn-farmer puzzle, zebra-puzzle, tower-of-hanoi, sudoku, slitherlink, other pencil puzzles, 8-sliding puzzle, 8-queens, knights move, Tic-tac-toe, 4-coloring map, and a few more.

So the first thing I realised was that many simple "classic" AI problems don't need much reasoning and can be solved with tree-search, constraint propogation, and state-hashing and backtracking. Basically brute force. And this is not to be overlooked as it forms the backbone of any algorithm.

The second thing I realised was that it is easy to find counter examples for which this breaks. The simplest example is this:

A 100x100 white grid with 2 red squares and 2 green squares.

Legal move: when a red square is next to any other, turn that square red and the original red square white.

Win: No green squares left.

Just using tree-search and state-hashing is infeasible. The key to this is, I believe, is recognition of the problem. We have to recognise that this can be interpreted as 2 red agents and 2 goals. Then pick an algorithm (A* search with distance heuristic) to solve.

Other more general techniques are:

(1) Invariant finding: Noticing all moves fix the number of red squraes at 2 and green squares can only deplete. [This can be a bit tricky since some things are invariant for a certain time only]

(2) Splitting the problem: We notice we can pair up each red square with each green square and solve this as two concurrent puzzles. Also hard to recognise.

Some other observations:

People have studied this area in

(1) General Game Playing (GGP)

(2) Planning Problems (PDDL/STRIPS)

One general thing from PDDL is the idea of ignoring delete lists to get a good admissible heuristic.

One of the hardest games to solve that is just at the edge of human solvability is Sokoban.

The general idea is just like there is not one general algorithm to solve any math problem, there will not be any one algorithm to solve any puzzle. So the idea is to use recognition and mix-and-match domain specific algorithms.

ARC-3 is a bit different in that you have to infer the rules. But once inferred you still have to have a good algorithm to solve it. So it's two hard problems in one!
